To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
alpha-amino acids are peculiarly resistant toward hydrogen atom abstraction by oxygen and chlorine radicals.

the backbone and side chain positions of alpha-amino acid residues are peculiarly stable toward hydrogen atom transfer, that this is true for both free amino acids and their peptides, and that this is a general phenomenon that applies to all types of alpha-amino residues.

the relative reactivity toward radical attack of different positions in alpha-amino acids and peptides is remarkably constant, and this pattern of reactivity is the basis for the unusual stability of these compounds in radical environments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of photochemical techniques for studying the reactivity and selectivity of radical intermediates in biological systems.
understanding the chemical and biochemical reactions of free radicals, particularly those that occur in biological systems.
free radical reactions in biology and the chemistry of the amino acids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the backbone and the alpha carbon of amino acids are resistant to hydrogen abstraction, but the side chains of the amino acids are not.
amino acids are peculiarly stable toward hydrogen atom abstraction and, in consequence, toward free radical reactions.
the backbone and the side chain positions of alpha-amino acid and peptide residues are peculiarly resistant toward hydrogen atom abstraction by radicals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
amino acids and their peptides are remarkably stable toward free radical reactions, but they do react.
free and N-acetylated amino acids and peptides, as well as the enzymes that utilize them, are remarkably resistant to free radical damage.

free and N-acetylated alpha-amino acids are peculiarly stable to hydrogen atom abstraction by radicals and this stability is a property of the backbone and the adjacent side chain positions, but not of other parts of the molecule.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reactivity of the amino acids and peptides toward free radicals is not the same as that of other organic molecules, and this is important for the design of synthetic methods for these compounds.
free radical chemistry of peptides and proteins is not as simple as one would expect from a study of the reactivity of the individual amino acids.
